note: NPR1/GC-A agonists (nesiritide, ularitide, cenderitide) in acute or chronic heart failure; the class relied on the dog (rapid-pacing HF, and healthy dogs for CD-NP) for cardiorenal predictions.
label: Heart failure (NP agonists)

engagement.note: ANP infused into pacing-HF dogs raised cGMP exactly as in healthy dogs; no patient comparison published.
engagement.short: ANP raises cGMP in HF dogs
engagement.quote: We found no difference between healthy dogs and animals with heart failure with respect to the secretion of c-GMP during ANP infusions in relation to the plasma levels of ANP.

engagement.note: CD-NP raised plasma and urinary cGMP in healthy volunteers as in dogs; the authors state the canine proved predictive.
engagement.short: CD-NP cGMP rise reproduced in humans
engagement.quote: Thus, the favorable in vivo responses observed in preclinical studies on CD-NP were indeed translated to human subjects.
engagement.judgement: Open-access full text read. Same group (Mayo) wrote the dog paper (Lisy 2008, doi:10.1016/j.jacc.2008.02.077) and the first-in-human; the comparison is stated in the source. Healthy volunteers, not patients, hence the 2018 entry.

engagement.note: In stable chronic HF patients a 4-h cenderitide infusion raised plasma and urinary cGMP, the engagement the dog work predicted.
engagement.short: cGMP rise confirmed in HF patients
engagement.quote: Four-hour infusion of Cenderitide was safe, well-tolerated, and significantly increased plasma cGMP levels and urinary cGMP excretion without adverse effects with no change in blood pressure.
engagement.judgement: Status unchanged from 2009; entry added because subjects change from healthy volunteers to HF patients, which a re-score may weight differently. Abstract only (paywalled); abstract calls the result the 'expected pharmacological effects'. Probable registry record NCT00620308 (Mayo, stable chronic HF; first posted 2008-02-21) has no results posted.

dose.note: Dog HF dose-ranging (0.01-0.3 ug/kg/min ANP) existed, but no model-to-patient exposure comparison was published; nesiritide's dose came from human dose-ranging.
dose.quote: The response of hemodynamic, renal, and hormonal variables was investigated after incremental infusions (0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, and 0.06 microgram/kg/min) of exogenous ANP.

dose.note: The dog's renal-active, mildly hypotensive 50 ng/kg/min dose was not tolerated: humans had symptomatic orthostatic hypotension at 25 and an MTD of 17.5.
dose.quote: At 25 ng/kg/min, 2 of the 4 subjects had symptomatic orthostatic hypotension following a diuretic response to CD-NP.
dose.reason: Dog-tolerated dose not tolerated in humans
dose.judgement: Judgement call. Lisy 2008 (doi:10.1016/j.jacc.2008.02.077, full text) infused healthy anesthetized dogs at 10, 50 and 100 ng/kg/min and called the 50 ng/kg/min dose 'less hypotensive' than BNP with a GFR rise; Lee 2009 planned 10-300 ng/kg/min but set the MTD at 17.5 ng/kg/min after orthostatic hypotension at 25 (~3x below the dog dose). Neither paper frames this as a dose-translation failure (the source calls the overall translation predictive), so comparison_stated is false; anesthetized supine dogs vs upright humans is the likely reason. Alternative reading: untested.

efficacy.note: Pacing-HF dogs lost ANP's natriuresis while keeping the cGMP rise: the model flagged renal resistance before any patient comparison.
efficacy.short: ANP natriuresis lost in HF dogs
efficacy.quote: The excretory effects on the kidneys were completely absent, and smaller increases in glomerular filtration rate and filtration fraction were observed.

efficacy.note: BNP cut filling pressure and raised natriuresis in pacing-HF dogs (Grantham 1997); nesiritide cut PCWP 5.8 mm Hg in VMAC, the approval trial.
efficacy.short: PCWP fall in dogs matched in VMAC
efficacy.quote: When added to standard care in patients hospitalized with acutely decompensated CHF, nesiritide improves hemodynamic function and some self-reported symptoms more effectively than intravenous nitroglycerin or placebo.
efficacy.judgement: My juxtaposition: model side is Grantham 1997 (doi:10.1152/ajpregu.1997.272.4.R1077; canine BNP 10 ng/kg/min in pacing AHF dogs: cGMP 65 vs 18 pg/ml, PCWP 9.1 vs 12.9 mmHg, natriuresis up). Patient-side hemodynamics were already known from Yoshimura 1991 (doi:10.1161/01.cir.84.4.1581; BNP 0.1 ug/kg/min, PCWP 21->14 mm Hg), i.e. the dog HF model post-dicted rather than predicted. Dogs received canine BNP, not nesiritide (product_in_model false). VMAC predates registry results posting.

efficacy.note: The model's cardiorenal benefit did not become clinical benefit: no effect on death/rehospitalization, dyspnea or renal function; ularitide repeated the null (TRUE-AHF 2017).
efficacy.short: No clinical or renal benefit in 7,141 patients
efficacy.quote: Nesiritide was not associated with an increase or a decrease in the rate of death and rehospitalization and had a small, nonsignificant effect on dyspnea when used in combination with other therapies.
efficacy.judgement: Judgement call. The dog papers the class relied on claimed renal enhancement (Chen 2004 doi:10.1152/ajpregu.00682.2004: BNP raised GFR 27->52 ml/min in overt pacing HF; Lisy 2008 'GFR enhancing'); ASCEND-HF found no renal benefit (eGFR fall >25%: 31.4 vs 29.5%) and no clinical benefit. TRUE-AHF (Packer 2017, doi:10.1056/NEJMoa1601895, NCT01661634, no registry results posted) found the same for ularitide: CV death HR 1.03 despite lower SBP and NT-proBNP. Caveat: Chen 2009 (doi:10.1016/j.jacc.2009.01.030) showed that at the clinical 0.01 ug/kg/min dose the HF dog gave only a trend in natriuresis/GFR, so the model run at the clinical dose was closer to the patients than the high-dose papers were; and mortality was never modelled. Alternative reading: 'same' on the hemodynamic surrogate with the model silent on outcomes. ASCEND-HF registry: NCT00475852, results first posted 2012-05-10.

safety.note: The dog model's only safety signal was a fall in arterial pressure; no patient comparison published.
safety.quote: In dogs with heart failure ANP caused a small reduction in mean arterial pressure.

safety.note: Meta-analysis of 5 trials: nesiritide raised the risk of worsening renal function (RR 1.52), the opposite of the model's renal enhancement.
safety.short: Renal worsening signal, model said enhancement
safety.quote: Nesiritide significantly increases the risk of worsening renal function in patients with ADHF.
safety.judgement: Source is a peer-reviewed meta-analysis of patient RCTs (1,269 patients), not a single trial; flagged in case the rules exclude meta-analyses. Abstract only.

safety.note: ASCEND-HF: no excess renal impairment (the 2005 signal did not hold), but more hypotension, the one adverse effect the dog model showed.
safety.short: Hypotension as in dogs; renal scare refuted
safety.quote: It was not associated with a worsening of renal function, but it was associated with an increase in rates of hypotension.
safety.reason: Hypotension as in dogs; renal scare refuted
safety.judgement: Judgement call: status moves contra -> same because the 7,141-patient trial superseded the 2005 meta-analysis on renal harm (eGFR fall >25%: 31.4 vs 29.5%, OR 1.09). Hypotension in dogs: Chen 2009 (systemic BNP caused 'a significant decrease in mean arterial pressure' in HF dogs) and Riegger 1988. For CD-NP, Lee 2009 states 'as in studies in the dog, the observed reductions in blood pressure were minimal' (healthy volunteers), though the dose cell records the orthostatic hypotension that capped the human dose. TRUE-AHF likewise saw greater SBP reductions with ularitide.
